answer.label: Not Kahlil Gibran — a 20th-century American saying
answer.authorDates: Origin unidentified — earliest documented version dates to 1969, 38 years after Gibran's death
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording traces to an anonymous college student’s saying published by educator Jess Lair in 1969 and popularized by artist Peter Max in 1972 — not to Kahlil Gibran, who died in 1931. It does not appear in any of Gibran’s published books or letters, and is absent from Wikiquote’s lists of both his sourced and his misattributed quotes.

source.excerpt: If you want something very, very badly, let it go free. If it comes back to you, it’s yours forever. If it doesn’t come back, it was never yours to begin with.
trail: In 1969, an anonymous college student handed educator Jess Lair a saying that became the documented ancestor of this quote, printed in his book I Ain’t Much, Baby—But I’m All I’ve Got ↗.
Graphic artist Peter Max popularized a shorter version in his syndicated 1972 “Meditation” comic panel, crediting it only to “Unknown” — see Quote Investigator’s research ↗.
By the 1990s the same saying had been wrongly attached to novelist Richard Bach, a claim Quote Investigator found no evidence for ↗.

The reworded “let them go…they were always yours” version now circulates online credited to Kahlil Gibran on Goodreads ↗, though no book, letter, or edition is ever cited, and it is absent from Gibran’s Wikiquote page ↗ entirely.
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented ancestor of the modern quote, as recorded by Jess Lair in 1969 — not Gibran’s wording, and not this exact phrasing.

author.bio: No single author has ever been credibly identified. Quote researcher Garson O’Toole traced the earliest known version to an anonymous college student who gave the saying to educator Jess Lair around 1969; it was popularized in 1972 by graphic artist Peter Max, who credited it only to “Unknown.” The saying was later wrongly attached to novelist Richard Bach, and more recently to Kahlil Gibran.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most-recycled “inspirational” sayings, and Kahlil Gibran is only its latest false author.

items.why: Goodreads, BrainyQuote, and similar sites credit Gibran with no book, letter, or edition ever cited; Goodreads itself notes ↗ such quotes are community-submitted and unverified.
Quote Investigator found no evidence ↗ that Bach ever wrote or used the phrase, though it circulated under his name for years.
The quote appears in neither Gibran’s sourced quotes nor his misattributed-quotes section ↗, meaning even dedicated quote-checkers haven’t linked it to him.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying’s real root is an anonymous American student’s note from 1969 — nearly four decades after Gibran died in 1931 — as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: A saying that keeps changing authors
lead: The “if you love something, set it free” family of sayings is one of the most persistent pieces of American folk wisdom, cycling through posters, comic panels, celebrity interviews, and now social media for over fifty years — each new era reattaching it to a bigger name.

Kahlil Gibran, whose 1923 book The Prophet made him one of the best-selling poets in American history, is a natural magnet for this kind of relabeling: his real writing is aphoristic and quotable enough that invented lines blend in easily.
detailsBody: 1969 — An anonymous college student gives educator Jess Lair the saying “If you want something very, very badly, let it go free. If it comes back to you, it’s yours forever,” printed in Lair’s book I Ain’t Much, Baby—But I’m All I’ve Got.
1972 — Artist Peter Max runs a shortened version in his syndicated “Meditation” comic panel, crediting it to “Unknown.”
1975–1978 — The saying spreads through Reader’s Digest, a photo caption in basketball player Bill Walton’s office, and an interview with actor Lee Majors.

1990s onward — The phrase is wrongly credited to novelist Richard Bach, and in more recent decades to Kahlil Gibran, in the reworded “let them go…they were always yours” form used on quote sites today.
context.pull: Gibran died in 1931 — 38 years before this saying's earliest documented trace.
